passages.title: Snow Day
sentences: Snow fell all night.
In the morning, the radio said school was closed.
Sam cheered.
He ran outside with Pixel and threw snowballs.
Grandma Rose looked out the window and sighed.
Her car was under a big pile of snow.
She had to dig it out to get to the bakery.
Sam saw her and got a second shovel.

passages.title: Rain on Match Day
sentences: The Gulls had a big soccer match on Saturday.
But on Saturday morning, rain poured down, and the field turned to mud.
The coach sent a text to say the match was canceled.
Ana stared at the rain on the window.
She had practiced her corner kicks all week.
"Now I have to wait two more weeks," she said.
Ben was on the couch with his game controller.
He was tired from a long week of tests.
He smiled and pulled a blanket over his legs.
"A rest day sounds great to me," he said.
The twins looked at each other.
It was the same rain, but they felt two different ways.

passages.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
sentences: A country mouse lived in a quiet field.
One day, his cousin from the town came to visit.
The country mouse served beans, corn and cool water.
"This food is so plain," said the town mouse. "Come to town with me!"
In town, the mice ate cake and cheese at a big table.
But the house was loud.
Doors banged, dogs barked, and people walked past all night.
The country mouse jumped at every bang.
"I love the bright lights and the fancy food," said the town mouse.
"I would rather eat beans in a quiet place," said the country mouse.
The next morning, he went home to his field.

credit.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Ferry Ride
sentences: On Friday, Sam took the ferry to his cousin's town by himself for the first time.
His mom walked him to the dock and gave him his ticket.
"Aunt Lucy will meet you on the other side," she said.
Sam had wanted to do this for months.
He had studied the ferry map and knew every stop.
As the ferry pulled away, he grinned and waved.
Then his stomach felt tight.
He checked his ticket three times.
He looked at the clock on the wall again and again.
What if Aunt Lucy was late?
Sam took out his map and found the dock where he would get off.
When the ferry bumped the dock, he saw Aunt Lucy waving.
He let out a long breath and waved back.

passages.title: Kai's News
sentences: Ben's best friend, Kai, lived two houses away.
They walked to school together every day.
One night, Kai came over with big news.
His mom had a new job in a city far up the coast, and they were moving in June.
Kai talked fast about his new house.
It had a big yard and a room just for him.
Then he got quiet.
"I'll miss walking to school with you," he said.
Ben looked at the floor.
His throat felt tight, and he stayed quiet for a long time.
Then he had an idea.
"We can play our game online every Friday," he said.
Kai smiled. "And you can visit me in the summer."
They shook hands.

passages.title: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
sentences: A fisherman sat on the rocks by the sea from morning until evening.
All day long, he caught only one fish, and it was very small.
As he reached for his basket, the little fish spoke.
"Please put me back in the sea," it said. "I am too small to make a good supper."
"If you let me go, I will grow big and fat."
"Then you can come back next year and catch me again."
The fisherman thought about this for a while.
"You may be right that you will grow," he said. "But I am hungry tonight."
"The sea is very big, and I may never find you again."
"A small supper tonight is better than a big supper that I might never get."
So he put the little fish in his basket and walked home.

credit.title: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Solo
sentences: Every spring, the Harbor Middle School band performs a concert in the gym, and one song includes a short solo that can be played on any instrument.
This year, Maya and Leo both auditioned for it.
On Friday afternoon, the band teacher pinned a list to the music room door.
Next to the word "Solo," it said "Maya Brooks."
Maya read the list twice.
She grinned, and then she pressed her hand against her stomach.
She had wanted this solo since September, but she had never performed alone in front of three hundred people.
"What if my hands start shaking?" she whispered.
Leo was standing right behind her, and he read the list too.
He had practiced the solo every evening for two weeks.
For a moment, he looked down at his shoes without saying anything.
Then he tapped Maya on the shoulder.
"Honestly, you played it better than I did," he said. "I am happy for you, and I am also a little disappointed."
Maya nodded slowly. "I am excited, and I am nervous too," she admitted.
"Could you sit somewhere I can see you on concert night?"
Leo grinned. "I will be at the drums, right behind the flutes," he said. "That is where I always sit."

passages.title: The Robot at the Café
sentences: On Monday, the Lighthouse Café got a new helper: a robot that carried plates from the kitchen to the tables.
It was about as tall as a kitchen stool and had three shelves for plates.
Sensors on its front helped it stop before it bumped into a chair or a person.
When it reached the right table, it played a short tune and waited for the customer to lift off the food.
Priya came in after school and watched it for half an hour.
She drew a map of its path around the tables and timed each trip with her watch.
"It turns so smoothly," she said. "I want to build one like it for the robot fair."
Grandma Rose came in later for her usual cup of tea, but she did not smile at the robot.
For years, Mrs. Lin, the owner, had carried the tea over herself and stopped to chat.
Now the robot rolled up, played its tune and waited.
"It is clever," Grandma Rose said, "but it does not ask me how the bakery is doing."
Mrs. Lin felt two ways about the robot.
She no longer had to carry heavy trays across the room, so her back did not ache at the end of the day.
But she missed stopping at each table for a quick chat.
So she made a new plan: the robot would carry the plates, and she would walk over afterward to say hello.
The next day, Grandma Rose got her tea from the robot and a friendly chat from Mrs. Lin.

passages.title: Lights Out at Nine
sentences: For many years, the night sky above Harbor Town had a dull orange glow.
Bright street lights, shop signs and the floodlights at the skate park sent light upward into the sky as well as down onto the ground.
Scientists call this light pollution.
The extra light makes the whole sky glow, and that glow hides fainter stars from view.
Astronomers at the observatory on Lantern Peaks noticed that they could see fewer stars every year.
In March, the town council voted to approve a new dark-sky plan.
Every street light would get a metal shield that aimed its light down at the ground instead of up at the sky.
Shop signs would switch off automatically at ten o'clock every evening.
The floodlights at the skate park, which used to stay on until eleven, would now switch off at nine.
Maya was thrilled, because she loved to draw the constellations, and the astronomers predicted that the town would soon see many more stars.
Leo was not thrilled at all.
In summer, he usually skated until the floodlights went out, because the evenings were cool and the park was quiet.
"Now I lose two hours of skating every night," he complained to Maya. "The stars were fine before."
"The stars were not fine," Maya replied. "We just could not see most of them."
On the first night of the new plan, Maya invited Leo to walk up to the lookout with her after the skate park closed.
When they reached the top of the hill, Leo stopped walking and stared upward in silence.
A pale band of light stretched across the entire sky, made by the light of billions of distant stars.
"Is that the Milky Way?" he asked, and Maya nodded.
On the walk home, Leo admitted that the sky was amazing, but he still wished the skate park had one more hour of light.
Maya suggested that they could ask the council for special lamps that shine only down onto the ramps.

passages.title: A Mine by the River
sentences: Copper is a reddish metal that is found in certain kinds of rock under the ground.
It carries electricity well, so it is used in phone chargers, computers, electric cars and the wires inside our homes.
To get copper, a company digs a mine, crushes the rock and separates the metal from the stone.
When a company plans a new mine near a town, people in the town often feel very differently about it.
Some people are glad, because a mine brings jobs that pay well, and the money helps local shops, schools and roads.
Young people who might have moved away to find work may be able to stay near their families.
Other people are worried.
Mines can be noisy and dusty, and big trucks carry rock along roads where children walk to school.
If waste from a mine leaks into a river, it can harm fish and the water that people and farms need.
Some people also love the forests and hills as they are, and they do not want them dug up.
Many people feel both ways at once.
A worker might want a job at the mine but also want to keep fishing in a clean river with her children.
To protect the land and water, many places have rules for mines.
In those places, a mine must test the water often, and when it closes, the company must cover the bare ground with soil and plant new trees and grass.
Before a new mine is allowed to open, people in the town can often go to public meetings, ask questions and share their views.
Hearing every side does not make the choice easy, but it can help a town make a choice that more people can accept.
